newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Doctor says Yeltsin's surgery may be delayed.
newsitem.headline: Doctor says Yeltsin's surgery may be delayed.

text.p: One of the doctors preparing Boris Yeltsin for heart surgery said the planned operation on the 65-year-old Russian president could be delayed and might have to be abandoned altogether.
Renat Akchurin said in a television interview that the possible success of the bypass surgery needed to improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart depended on an analysis of his current condition.

Yeltsin, who has a history of heart problems, has disappeared almost completely from public view since late June when he was elected to a second term in the Kremlin after conducting a vigorous campaign across the vast country.
He said in a televised interview earlier this month that he needed heart surgery and had agreed to undergo the operation, probably in late September.
But Akchurin, chosen to head a team of 12 surgeons to carry out the operation, was asked on NTV commercial television when it would take place and replied: "Within 1-1/2 or two months."

He said a group of Russian and foreign doctors was due to decide on Wednesday or Thursday when and whether it would be safe to operate on Yeltsin, who is now undergoing tests in Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital.
"We will see how the patient is prepared for the operation. Any risk should be justified. If the risk is justified, go and do the operation. If it is not, don't do silly things," Akchurin said.
"We need to go throught a certain preparatory period and Yeltsin, who whips us up all the time, seems to understand this. An earlier date of the operation means bigger risks."

Asked whether the operation might have to be abandoned, Akchurin said: "It is possible but special conditions should be created for the president then. We would be forced to limit his physical activities. He is not going to tolerate this."

Yeltsin has issued a decree confirming that Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, his constitutional deputy, will govern if he is incapacitated but he appears reluctant to loosen his grip on power for any substential period of time.
Kremlin sources says he is likely to transfer his powers, including a control over the "nuclear button", for only for a few hours while he is unconscious in the operation theatre.
Yeltsin's daughter Tatyana, who is looking after him, told Russian television that he was keeping an eye on all major developments.
"He is attentively listening to reports about who called him and what was the message," she said. "He reads newspapers and he knows everything they say about him."
